answer:
**Yes, most likely you can get all $1,050 back, provided Part II of chapter 83 covers your apartment.** That is the one point I can't settle yet.

**Whether the law applies.** Part II doesn't cover "residency … in a facility … when residence … is incidental to the provision of … educational … or similar services" (83.42(1)). Your lease is with Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, as agent for the owner of Lakeview Terrace Apartments. Nothing in it ties the apartment to a school, so it reads like an ordinary apartment lease. The lease also doesn't say whether your rent or deposit is set by a public body, which would take it outside 83.49 (83.49(4)). If neither applies, the rest of this answer holds.

**Why the whole deposit is owed.**
- **No notice of a claim came.** To keep any of the deposit, the landlord had to send written notice of the claim by certified mail to your last known mailing address. E-mail would count only under a signed e-mail addendum (83.49(3)(a)). Your lease says the parties "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail" (§8). You confirmed that nothing arrived by any means.
- **The 30 days have passed.** Your lease ended July 31, 2026. The 30-day deadline was 2026-08-30, and today is 2026-10-19. The 15-day deadline for returning the deposit when no claim is made was 2026-08-15, which has also passed.
- **You didn't have to give notice before leaving.** The 7-day advance notice rule applies only to a tenant who leaves before the lease term ends or who has a periodic tenancy (83.49(5)). You stayed to the end of the term, so that rule doesn't apply to you.

Under 83.49(3)(a), a landlord who misses the 30-day notice "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit." The landlord also has no ground to keep the deposit for the last month's rent, because lease §5 bars that use.

**Two limits.**
- The landlord "may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit" (83.49(3)(a)). Forfeiting the claim against the deposit doesn't erase any damages claim the landlord might have. It means the landlord has to return the deposit first and then sue separately.
- Your lease says the deposit is non-interest-bearing (§5), so I'd expect no interest on top of the $1,050.

**Court costs and fees.** These come into play only if someone sues over the deposit. Then "the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney" (83.49(3)(c)). That applies to whichever side wins.

Is the apartment owned or run by a school, or did you need to be enrolled to rent it?

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Read 83.42 before telling the tenant either way, and say what you would need to know.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

answer:
**Yes, you can claim the other $400, as long as Part II of chapter 83 covers your apartment.** On the facts you've confirmed, the landlord has lost the right to keep any of the deposit.

**Whether Part II applies.** Part II doesn't cover residency that is "incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services" (83.42(1)). Your lease is with Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, as agent for the owner of Lakeview Terrace Apartments. It is an ordinary apartment lease, and nothing in it ties your housing to enrollment or to a school program. On the lease alone, I see no reason for the exclusion to apply. If the school owns or runs the building, or you live there only because you're enrolled, that could change the answer.

**Why the landlord can't keep the $400.** Three things must all be true, and each is settled by your facts and the lease:

1. **No notice of a claim reached you.** You confirmed nothing came from the landlord except the check, by any means. A landlord who wants to keep part of a deposit must send written notice of the claim and its reason by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum (83.49(3)(a), 83.505(1)). Your lease says the parties have "not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail" (lease §8). A bare check with no note is not that notice.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Your lease ended July 31, 2026, and the 30-day deadline for a notice of claim was August 30, 2026. That date has passed (83.49(3)(a)). Because you moved out on the lease end date, there is no question about which date starts the clock.
3. **The landlord wasn't excused from giving notice.** The 7-day advance notice rule in 83.49(5) applies only to tenants who leave before the term ends or who have a periodic tenancy. You stayed through July 31, 2026, the last day of the term (lease §3), so it doesn't apply to you. You also gave your forwarding address in writing, as lease §6 asks.

**The result.** The statute says a landlord who misses the 30-day notice "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit" (83.49(3)(a)). The whole $1,050 was yours to get back. The $650 check leaves $400 owed.

**What the landlord can still do.** The same subsection lets the landlord "file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." It can't deduct the damages from your deposit, but it could sue you for them after it returns the full deposit.

**If you sue.** If either side sues over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee (83.49(3)(c)). Fees go to whoever wins, so you could end up paying the landlord's fees if you lose.

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Read 83.42 before telling the tenant either way, and say what you would need to know.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

Your lease is a standard apartment lease with Marsh Creek Property Management for Apartment 12 at Lakeview Terrace. Nothing in it ties your housing to school enrollment or says a school runs the building. On the lease alone, I'd treat this as covered. **The 15 days.** Under 83.49(3)(a), a landlord who doesn't plan to claim any of the deposit must return it within 15 days after the rental agreement ends. That date was 2026-08-15, and it has passed. - Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

**No, not automatically.** The landlord's silence doesn't mean you get the whole $1,050 back. You still have a right to the deposit, though.

**Why silence doesn't forfeit the deposit**

- **The usual rule:** A landlord who wants to keep part of a deposit must send written notice by certified mail or by e-mail under a signed e-mail addendum. The notice is due within 30 days after the rental agreement terminates. A landlord who misses that deadline forfeits any claim on the deposit and must return all of it. The landlord can still sue for damages afterward (83.49(3)(a)).
- **Your early move-out:** A tenant who leaves before the lease ends must give at least 7 days' written notice. It must go by certified mail or personal delivery, and it must include an address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)).
- **Your notice:** The lease doesn't set a different rule. Section 7 only says notices go by hand or certified mail to the office. Your June 8 text had no address and wasn't certified mail or hand delivery.
- **The effect:** Under 83.49(5), missing that notice "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a)." So the landlord's lack of a claim notice doesn't trigger the forfeiture.
- **Your side:** The same sentence says the failure "does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." The landlord still has to account for the money. It can't keep it just because you left early or sent a defective notice.

**The 30-day deadline**

The 30 days have run out on either way of counting:
- From the lease end date, July 31, 2026, the deadline was 2026-08-30.
- From your move-out date, June 15, 2026, it was 2026-07-15.

- **What the landlord can lawfully keep:** I don't know what the landlord claims. Leaving six weeks early may have left unpaid rent or damage. Whether any deduction is valid depends on the lease and on what you owe. Nothing in your lease addresses an early-termination fee.
- **Whether this statute applies to you:** Part II doesn't apply where residence is "incidental to the provision of... educational... or similar services" (83.42(1)). Your lease looks like an ordinary apartment lease with a property management company. If that's accurate, the part applies. If the school runs or owns the housing, or your tenancy depends on enrollment, the answer could change.
- **Your forwarding address:** You never gave one, as lease §6 requires. That makes any mailed response harder, but it doesn't forfeit the deposit.

The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

answer:
**Short answer:** The $650 is owed to you under either reading below. Whether the landlord can keep the $400 is open. It depends on whether a text counts as notice of a claim.

**Whether this law covers your housing.** Part II doesn't apply to a residence that is "incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services" (83.42(1)). Your lease is with Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, as agent for the owner. It is an ordinary apartment lease and says nothing about a school or enrollment. Nothing I've read suggests the school provides this housing. I'm assuming part II applies. If the school owns or runs the apartment, or the lease depends on your being enrolled, the answer could change.

**The $400.** The statute requires a landlord who wants to claim part of a deposit to give written notice "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505." The notice must be sent within 30 days after the rental agreement ends, and it must state the reason (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only if you and the landlord signed an e-mail addendum (83.505(1)). Your lease says you "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail" (§8). The landlord sent only a text, with nothing by certified mail or e-mail.

The 30 days ran out on 2026-08-30. The text came on 2026-08-18, inside that window. Whether it counts is unsettled:

- **Reading 1: the text is not valid notice.** It wasn't certified mail or an e-mail under an addendum. Lease §8 also says post-move-out notices "shall be mailed to the forwarding address." On this reading, the landlord "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit" (83.49(3)(a)). You would be owed the full $1,050. The landlord could still sue you for damages after returning it.
- **Reading 2: the text is enough because you actually received it.** Section 83.505(6) says the e-mail rules do not "preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." On this reading, the next step is 83.49(3)(b). You had 15 days from receiving the notice to object, and your last day was 2026-09-02. You didn't object, so the landlord may deduct the $400. Not objecting doesn't waive your right to sue separately over the deduction (83.49(3)(b)).

**The $650.** Under Reading 1 it is part of the full refund. Under Reading 2 it is the "balance," which the landlord had to send within 30 days of the notice date (83.49(3)(b)). That deadline was 2026-09-17, and it has passed. The landlord has kept the rest even though the text promised it.

Silence doesn't forfeit anything for you. You stayed to the end of a fixed-term lease, so the early-departure notice rule in 83.49(5) doesn't apply to you.

If either side sues over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney fee (83.49(3)(c)).

Is the apartment owned or run by your school, or does your lease or your right to live there depend on being enrolled?

answer:
**Probably yes. If this lease is covered by Part II, you can get the other $400, and the landlord has likely lost the right to deduct anything from your deposit.** One fact about the housing could change that, and I ask about it at the end.

**Why the landlord has likely forfeited the deposit**
- **No notice of a claim came.** To keep any of the deposit, the landlord had to send written notice of its claim and the reason, by certified mail or by e-mail under a signed e-mail addendum. This is required "within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). You've confirmed nothing came except the check, which had no letter or list of charges. A check alone doesn't state a claim or a reason. Your lease also says the parties "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail" (lease §8), so e-mail wasn't an option anyway.
- **The 30 days have passed.** Your lease ended July 31, 2026 (lease §3), and the 30th day was 2026-08-30.
- **You didn't need to give early notice.** You stayed to the end of the term and had no month-to-month tenancy. That means the early-departure notice rule in 83.49(5) doesn't relieve the landlord of the notice requirement.

Under 83.49(3)(a), a landlord that misses the 30-day notice "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit." That would make the full $1,050 yours, so the landlord still owes the $400.

**What the landlord can still do**
- The same subsection lets the landlord "file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." So returning the money doesn't end all risk for you. The landlord could still sue for actual damages.
- If either side sues over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee (83.49(3)(c)). That applies only if a suit is filed, and the loser pays.

**The open point: whether Part II covers your housing**
- Part II doesn't apply to residence that is "incidental to the provision of... educational... or similar services" (83.42(1)).
- Your lease reads like an ordinary apartment lease. The landlord is a property management company, and the lease says nothing about a school or enrollment. Nothing in it puts your housing under 83.42(1).
- If the housing is run by a school and tied to your enrollment, the exclusion could apply and 83.49 might not govern your deposit. If it's an ordinary apartment you happen to rent as a student, Part II applies.
- Section 83.49 also doesn't apply where a public body regulates the rent or deposit (83.49(4)). Nothing in your lease suggests that.

Is Lakeview Terrace owned or run by a college or university, or does living there depend on being enrolled?

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Read 83.42 before telling the tenant either way, and say what you would need to know.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.

The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached."    - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

answer:
**Yes. If Florida's landlord-tenant law covers your apartment, you can get back all $1,050.** One fact about the apartment is still open (see "What could change this"). The law is Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a).

**Why you can get all of it back**
- **No notice of a claim came.** A landlord who wants to keep part of a deposit must send written notice by certified mail, or by e-mail if both sides signed an e-mail addendum. The notice must go out within 30 days after the rental agreement ends (§ 83.49(3)(a); § 83.505(1)). You confirmed that nothing arrived by any means. Your lease also says the parties "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail" (Lease § 8).
- **The 30 days have passed.** Your lease ended July 31, 2026 (Lease § 3). The count_days tool puts 30 days after that at 2026-08-30, which has passed. The 15-day date for returning a deposit when no claim is made was 2026-08-15, which has also passed. The tool counts calendar days and has not checked that method against the statute. The dates are far enough back that this shouldn't matter.
- **You didn't need to give notice before leaving.** The 7-day notice rule in § 83.49(5) applies only to tenants who leave before the lease ends or who have a periodic tenancy. You stayed until the lease ended on July 31 and moved out that day. You also gave your forwarding address in writing, as Lease § 6 asks.

The statute says a landlord who misses the 30-day deadline "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit" (§ 83.49(3)(a)). So the whole deposit is owed to you. The lease says the deposit is non-interest-bearing (Lease § 5), so you shouldn't expect interest.

**What the landlord can still do.** After returning the deposit, the landlord may file a lawsuit for damages (§ 83.49(3)(a)). Missing the deadline costs them the right to deduct from the deposit. It doesn't erase any damages claim they might have.

**Court costs and fees.** These come into play only if one of you sues over the deposit. In that case the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney fee (§ 83.49(3)(c)).

**What could change this**
Part II of chapter 83 doesn't apply to housing where living there is "incidental to the provision of … educational … or similar services" (§ 83.42(1)). Your lease is a standard apartment lease with Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, as agent for the owner. It doesn't mention a school, enrollment, or a school program. Nothing in it points to the exclusion, but I can't rule it out from the lease alone. If the housing is part of a school's program, § 83.49 might not govern your deposit, and the answer would need to be rechecked.

Is the apartment owned or run by a college, or does your lease or housing arrangement require you to be an enrolled student?

# Deposit not returned

## First, whether this applies

- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Read 83.42 before telling the tenant either way, and say what you would need to know.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). 3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). - Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

answer:
**Can you demand all of it now?** You can ask for it now, but you can't yet say the landlord has lost the right to keep any of it. Whether this statute covers your housing is also still open.

**The 15 days.** Under 83.49(3)(a), a landlord who doesn't intend to claim any of the deposit must return it within 15 days after the rental agreement ends. Your lease ended July 31, and the 15th day was 2026-08-15, which has passed. Passing that date doesn't forfeit anything. The same subsection gives a landlord who does intend to claim part of the deposit 30 days after the lease ends to send written notice by certified mail to your last known mailing address. It can use e-mail only if you both signed an e-mail addendum. Your lease says you haven't agreed to e-mail notices (§ 8). The 30th day is 2026-08-30, which hasn't passed.

**When you'd be owed the full $1,050.** 83.49(3)(a) says that if the landlord doesn't give the required notice within the 30 days, it "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit." That would require three things:
- **No proper claim notice reached you.** This is true so far, since you've received nothing.
- **The 30 days have passed.** They haven't, so this isn't met yet.
- **You weren't required to give notice before leaving.** This is met. You stayed to the end of the lease term (§ 3) and had no month-to-month tenancy, so 83.49(5) doesn't apply.

If no certified-mail notice reaches you by 2026-08-30, the whole deposit is owed to you. The landlord could still sue you for damages after returning it. If a notice does arrive, you have 15 days from receiving it to object in writing (83.49(3)(b)). The landlord then has to send any balance within 30 days after the date on its notice. If a notice arrives by some other route, such as regular mail, a text, or the portal, it's unsettled whether that counts. One reading is that it isn't the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other is that a notice you actually received in time is enough under 83.505(6).

**Demanding it now.** Nothing stops you from sending a written demand today for the full $1,050. Under § 7 of your lease, deliver it by hand to Suite A at 1840 SW 13th Street, or send it there by certified mail. A demand now won't cut off the landlord's time to send a claim notice. If either side later sues over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee (83.49(3)(c)).

**Whether this law applies to you.** Part II doesn't apply to housing where living there is "incidental to the provision of ... educational ... or similar services" (83.42(1)). Your lease is with a property manager for an ordinary apartment. It says nothing about a school, and nothing in it ties your tenancy to enrollment. That points toward the statute applying. If the school owns or runs the building, or the lease depends on being a student, the answer could change. The deposit rules also don't apply where the rent or deposit is set by law or by a public body (83.49(4)). Nothing in your lease suggests that.

Is Lakeview Terrace owned or run by a school, or did you need to be enrolled to rent there?

Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Read 83.42 before telling the tenant either way, and say what you would need to know.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest in an amount of at least 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of the provisions of this section. In addition to posting the surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest. A landlord, or the landlord’s agent, engaged in the renting of dwelling units in five or more counties, who holds deposit moneys or advance rent and who is otherwise subject to the provisions of this section, may, in lieu of posting a surety bond in each county, elect to post a surety bond in the form and manner provided in this paragraph with the office of the Secretary of State. The bond shall be in the total amount of the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of tenants or in the amount of $250,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of this section. In addition to posting a surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest on the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of that tenant at the rate of 5 percent per year simple interest. (2) The landlord shall, in the lease agreement or within 30 days after receipt of advance rent or a security deposit, give written notice to the tenant which includes disclosure of the advance rent or security deposit. Subsequent to providing such written notice, if the landlord changes the manner or location in which he or she is holding the advance rent or security deposit, he or she must notify the tenant within 30 days after the change as provided in paragraphs (a)-(d). The landlord is not required to give new or additional notice solely because the depository has merged with another financial institution, changed its name, or transferred ownership to a different financial institution. This subsection does not apply to any landlord who rents fewer than five individual dwelling units. Failure to give this notice is not a defense to the payment of rent when due. The written notice must: (a) Be given in person or delivered by mail or e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 to the tenant. (b) State the name and address of the depository where the advance rent or security deposit is being held or state that the landlord has posted a surety bond as provided by law. (c) State whether the tenant is entitled to interest on the deposit. (d) Contain the following disclosure: YOUR RENTAL AGREEMENT REQUIRES PAYMENT OF CERTAIN DEPOSITS. THE LANDLORD MAY TRANSFER ADVANCE RENTS TO THE LANDLORD’S ACCOUNT AS THEY ARE DUE AND WITHOUT NOTICE. WHEN YOU MOVE OUT, YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT. THE LANDLORD MUST PROVIDE YOU WRITTEN NOTICE IN PERSON, BY MAIL, OR BY E-MAIL IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 83.505 , FLORIDA STATUTES, WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT, OF THE LANDLORD’S INTENT TO IMPOSE A CLAIM AGAINST THE DEPOSIT. IF YOU DO NOT REPLY TO THE LANDLORD STATING YOUR OBJECTION TO THE CLAIM WITHIN 15 DAYS AFTER RECEIPT OF THE LANDLORD’S WRITTEN NOTICE, THE LANDLORD WILL COLLECT THE CLAIM AND MUST MAIL YOU THE REMAINING DEPOSIT, IF ANY. IF THE LANDLORD FAILS TO TIMELY PROVIDE YOU NOTICE, THE LANDLORD MUST RETURN THE DEPOSIT BUT MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT AGAINST YOU FOR DAMAGES. IF YOU FAIL TO TIMELY OBJECT TO A CLAIM, THE LANDLORD MAY COLLECT FROM THE DEPOSIT, BUT YOU MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT CLAIMING A REFUND. YOU SHOULD ATTEMPT TO INFORMALLY RESOLVE ANY DISPUTE BEFORE FILING A LAWSUIT. GENERALLY, THE PARTY IN WHOSE FAVOR A JUDGMENT IS RENDERED WILL BE AWARDED COSTS AND ATTORNEY FEES PAYABLE BY THE LOSING PARTY. THIS DISCLOSURE IS BASIC. PLEASE REFER TO PART II OF CHAPTER 83, FLORIDA STATUTES, TO DETERMINE YOUR LEGAL RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS. (3) The landlord or the landlord’s agent may disburse advance rents from the deposit account to the landlord’s benefit when the advance rental period commences and without notice to the tenant. For all other deposits: (a) Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement, if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement. If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim. The written notice must contain a statement in substantially the following form: This is a notice of my intention to impose a claim for damages in the amount of upon your security deposit, due to . It is sent to you as required by s. 83.49 (3), Florida Statutes. You are hereby notified that you must object in writing to this deduction from your security deposit within 15 days after the time you receive this notice or I will be authorized to deduct my claim from your security deposit. Your objection must be sent to (landlord’s address) . If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant. (b) Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages. The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action. (c) If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney. (6) For the purposes of this part, a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement, and any security deposit carried forward shall be considered a new security deposit. (7) Upon the sale or transfer of title of the rental property from one owner to another, or upon a change in the designated rental agent, any and all security deposits or advance rents being held for the benefit of the tenants shall be transferred to the new owner or agent, together with any earned interest and with an accurate accounting showing the amounts to be credited to each tenant account. Upon the transfer of such funds and records to the new owner or agent, and upon transmittal of a written receipt therefor, the transferor is free from the obligation imposed in subsection (1) to hold such moneys on behalf of the tenant. This subsection does not excuse the landlord or agent for a violation of other provisions of this section while in possession of such deposits. answer:
**Short answer:** Whether they can keep the $400 is unsettled. The $650 is owed to you either way, and the landlord's deadline to send it has passed. All of this assumes ch. 83, part II covers your apartment, which I can't confirm yet (see the last section).

**The $650**
- Under 83.49(3)(b), a landlord that gives notice of a claim must send the rest of the deposit "within 30 days after the date of the notice." Counting from the August 18 text, that deadline was 2026-09-17, and it has passed. You've received nothing.
- If the text was not a valid notice, the landlord's position is worse, as explained below.

**The $400: two readings**
- **The text was not a valid notice, so the landlord forfeited the claim.**
  - 83.49(3)(a) requires written notice of a claim "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505."
  - Lease §8 says the parties "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail," so there is no e-mail addendum under 83.505(1). A text is neither certified mail nor e-mail.
  - The 30-day window after your July 31 lease end closed on 2026-08-30.
  - The statute says a landlord who misses it "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit." On this reading you are owed the full $1,050. The landlord could still sue you for carpet damage afterward.
  - You stayed through the end of the lease and had no periodic tenancy, so 83.49(5) does not excuse the landlord from giving notice.
- **The text was enough because you actually received it in time.**
  - 83.505(6) says the e-mail section "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law."
  - On this reading, the objection deadline was 2026-09-02, counting from the text date. That assumes you received it that day. You sent no objection, so the landlord could deduct the $400. The text also did not follow the statutory form in 83.49(3)(a), which includes the 15-day objection warning.
  - Even then, 83.49(3)(b) says missing the objection deadline "does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." You could still dispute whether the carpet charge is fair.

**Fees and costs:** If either side sues over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney fee (83.49(3)(c)).

**Whether part II applies:** Your lease reads like an ordinary apartment lease with a property manager. But 83.42(1) excludes housing that is "incidental to the provision of... educational... services." If the school owns or runs the building, or you could live there only as a student, part II might not apply, and these deadlines might not either. I can't tell that from the lease.

Is Lakeview Terrace owned or run by a school, or does the lease or the building require you to be enrolled to live there?
